title: Migrate legacy trails from local AI-tool transcripts
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Older Showtail trails often lack replies, edits, plans, decisions and tool calls that the AI tools still keep in their own local transcripts. This PR implements the plan "V1-to-V2 Transcript Migration and Upgrade Workflow": add an append-only migrator that enriches those trails, reachable through `showtail migrate` for the current project and through a one-time upgrade offer that scans the home directory for eligible projects.

**Design.** Each local coding tool plugin (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI/IDE, Copilot CLI, Copilot Chat) now declares a `migration` capability, and `migrationPlugins` in the registry collects them. The transcript readers were changed so migration can list a tool's sessions before filtering them to a project: previously the Claude Code reader skipped any transcript whose cwd did not match the project root, and it now skips those without a cwd; the Copilot Chat reader changed the same way. In migration mode the Antigravity CLI parser keeps CODE_ACTION file edits, which live reconcile still drops because the hook already snapshots them; a code comment notes the transcript keeps a file:// URI even when the file is gone. Recovered prompts, replies and other events are appended as new batch-tagged events alongside enrichment records and overlays, rather than rewriting existing journal entries, and each run is a batch that `migrate undo` can remove; `verify` treats a `migration-undo` marker like an `import-undo` one. `--dry-run` reports what could be recovered without writing a batch, and `--json` gives machine output; with `--json` and no `--yes` the preview and confirmation are skipped. Ambiguous candidates are counted per status and, in an interactive terminal, the user is asked to confirm them.

**Upgrade path.** `HISTORY_GENERATION` is now 2 and the global config records known project paths and upgrade state; commands like `init`, `status` and the hook note the project they run in. An existing generation-1 install gets one pending generation-2 offer, asked on the first command that is neither `migrate` nor a `--json` run, where Enter accepts. A machine with no prior global config is treated as a fresh install. Bulk discovery finds nested project trails and skips a home-directory catch-all, then migrates each eligible project independently and writes a manifest; if the bulk run throws, the offer is left in `running` state and is not offered again. The installers pass `--offer-migration` to first-run setup.

**Consequences and gaps.** The case-insensitive path comparison used on Windows and the `install.ps1` change were not run on Windows; the recorded runs were on linux/x64. The interactive confirmation prompts in `migrate` and the upgrade offer were not shown with a user at a terminal. Docs and the changelog describe the new command and data layout.

title: fix: launch extension CLIs through cmd on Windows
body:
## Summary
On Windows, VS Code-compatible CLIs (`code`, the Antigravity launcher) are installed as `.cmd` batch files. A direct `spawnSync` goes through CreateProcess, which can't run batch files. That includes a bare `code` that PATHEXT resolves to `code.cmd`. As a result, `--install-extension` failed on Windows.

- Adds `src/core/extensionCli.ts`:

- Adds unit tests for the invocation on Windows (bare `code` and a full `.cmd` path containing spaces) and on POSIX.

title: fix: launch extension CLIs through cmd on Windows
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR routes the VS Code and Antigravity extension launchers through the Windows command processor, so a Windows problem in those launchers no longer holds back a release from publishing artifacts.

Previously `installVsCodeExtension` and `installAntigravityIdeExtension` called `spawnSync` on the extension CLI directly with `--install-extension <payload> --force`. A code comment in the new module notes that Windows installs expose `code`-style CLIs as `.cmd` files, which a direct `spawnSync` cannot execute, even when a bare `code` resolves to `code.cmd` through PATHEXT.

## Design

`extensionCliInvocation` builds the command: when the target platform is `win32` it returns the command processor with `/d /c <cli> <args...>`, and on other platforms it returns the CLI and its arguments unchanged. The command processor comes from `ComSpec`, then `COMSPEC`, and falls back to `cmd.exe` when neither is set. `runExtensionCli` hands that invocation to `spawnSync`, and both installers now call it with the same `--install-extension … --force` arguments as before. The comment in the new module says each token stays a separate spawn argument so the runtime handles quoting of paths with spaces; note that the tokens after `/c` are then parsed again by `cmd.exe`.

The platform and command processor are parameters with defaults, so tests can check the Windows invocation on any host. `tests/vscodeExtension.test.ts` adds cases asserting that Windows launchers go through `cmd.exe` and that POSIX launchers run directly.

## Consequences

Success and failure handling in both installers is unchanged: they still branch on `status` from the spawn result. The new tests check the invocation that gets built, not a real Windows `.cmd` launch, and CI results for the pushed head are not recorded, so a real Windows `.cmd` launch is still unconfirmed.

## Validation

<sub>From runs on the submitted content.</sub>

- Checks passed on the submitted content: `bun run typecheck`, `bun run format:check`.
- `bun test`: failed (621 pass, 63 fail, Ran 688 tests across 94 files. [175.06s]), run on the submitted content.

Where to start: `extensionCliInvocation` in `src/core/extensionCli.ts`, which owns the Windows/POSIX split and the command-processor fallback.

title: feat(brief): owners rows say where each behavior lives; code cells spell out direction
body:
## Summary

The brief now tells the drafter **where** each behavior lives and **which direction** a code change went.

- **Owners rows.** These appear in the TOON brief, the neighborhood tail and lens A of the lean review packet. Each row maps a clause from the commit message to the one or two changed functions whose changed lines say it.
  - Hunks now record the words on each function's changed lines (`fnWords`). A changed doc comment counts toward the function defined below it. This keeps functions apart when one hunk defines several of them.
  - Scoring gives less weight to words that most functions share and a bonus to linked hunks. A clear lead is required before a row is emitted.
  - Rows appear only for change units where two or more functions own different sentences: at most 5 per unit and 6 in total. They never show call relations.
- **Direction in code cells.**
  - `added:` / `removed:` replace bare `+`/`-`, and before/after pairs read `was ... -> now ...`.
  - For a changed boolean condition, including multi-line chains, the cell lists the operands that were dropped, kept and added, in place of the bare removed fragments.
  - Value fallbacks such as `a || ref` stay as value changes.
  - Direction words don't count against the code-cell budget.
- **`drafting.md`** tells the drafter to read direction from code cells and to name where a behavior lives from the owners rows.

New tests are in `tests/brief-owners-direction.test.ts`, and the existing brief and graph-search expectations are updated.

- `bun run test`: 45 of 46 files passed. `tests/review-run.test.ts` had 11 tests hit the 5 s timeout during the 4-process concurrent run. Run alone (`bun test tests/review-run.test.ts`), all 17 pass. This looks like a timing problem under load, not a regression.
- `test:bundled` / `test:compiled`: left to CI, which runs the packaged contracts on every PR.

## Why

The goal of this PR is to "implement both fixes and rerun Claude and Codex": add an owners section that maps commit-sentence clauses to the one or two changed functions whose changed lines say them, and make code cells spell out direction so a writer can't read a removed line as added.

title: Record every check in a chained command, and keep the full merge base
body:
## Summary

**Every check in a chained command is now recorded.** Agents often chain several checks in one shell command, for example `bun run bundle; bun x tsc --noEmit && bun test > log; bun scripts/eval-summaries.ts`. Until now the digest recorded only the test run, and it kept every result line from the whole output. So the eval's "57/57 checks pass" got attached to the tests, and the bundle, typecheck and eval looked like they never ran. Agents writing PR descriptions from the digest then said those checks "were not run" when they had been.

- New `commandRuns()` in `src/digest/build.ts` returns one run per check in the command, in order (build, typecheck, lint, eval, test). `commandRun()` now returns the first of these, so existing callers behave the same.
- When a command runs several checks, each run keeps only the output lines of its own kind (`KIND_LINE`), so test counts and eval counts stay with their own runs.
- A failing exit status from a command with several checks is recorded as `unknown`, not `failed` on all of them, because we can't tell which check failed. A single check that fails is still `failed`.
- The existing rule for test commands is unchanged: several test-runner segments still make up one listed run with an `unknown` outcome.

**The digest keeps the full merge base.** `digest.json` stored the merge base cut to 12 characters, but `tracetoon source --revision base` needs the full hash. So that command always failed with "Code evidence must use the prepared base or head revision". The digest now stores the full hash.

**Bundle rebuilt.** `plugin/skills/tracetoon/dist/tracetoon.mjs` and `build.json` were regenerated with `bun run bundle`, as CONTRIBUTING requires for changes to `src/`.

## Tests

- `tests/evidence.test.ts`: a chained bundle → test → eval command gives three runs, each with only its own summary lines. A `&&` chain gives build, typecheck and test runs with the right segments. A failing chain gives `unknown` for every run, and a single failing typecheck still gives `failed`.
- `tests/preparation.test.ts`: `tracetoon source --revision base` resolves to a full 40-character hash and returns the base content.

## Verification (Bun 1.3.14, Linux)

- `bun run typecheck`: passed (exit 0)
- `bun run test`: 36 source test files passed, 0 failed (523 tests)
- `bun run bundle` then `bun run build:check`: passed, and the regenerated bundle is committed
- `bun run test:bundled`: passed, all 13 packaged contracts verified against the shipped bundle
- `bun run test:compiled`: not run locally. Left to CI, which runs the packaged contracts on every PR on every platform.

title: test: guard CLI calls and test files against Bun on Windows not exiting
body:
## Summary

Windows CI jobs hung for hours several times, each time in a different test file. The cause is Bun 1.3.14 on Windows: a process (the CLI under test, or `bun test` itself) prints its whole result and then never exits. This PR fixes the CLI where it can and makes the test harness tolerate the rest, so a hang fails within minutes instead of holding a runner.

**Product change**
- `src/cli.ts`: once stdout and stderr are flushed, the CLI calls `process.exit` with the command's exit code instead of waiting to exit on its own. If `$TRACETOON_EXIT_FILE` is set (only test harnesses set it), the CLI writes its exit code there first. It removes the variable from its own environment at startup, so processes it starts never inherit it.

**Test harness**
- `tests/spawn-guard.ts` (new): runs a command with inherited stdio. If the exit-code file appears and the process is still alive 3s later, the guard kills it (`taskkill /T /F` on Windows) and returns the recorded code. Commands that exit on their own, or never finish, behave as before.
- `tests/helpers.ts` (preloaded for every test file): mocks `node:child_process` so that `spawnSync(bun, [cli.ts | tracetoon.mjs, ...])` goes through the guard. That covers every test file that spawns the CLI, including `graph.test.ts`'s own helper.
- `scripts/test-files.ts`:
  - The runner kills a test file and its process tree after 15 minutes (`TRACETOON_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS`), prints what the file had output so far, and fails it.
  - Once a file has printed its summary line, the runner waits 20s for Bun to exit. If it doesn't, the runner kills it and takes the result from the summary's fail/error counts.
- `review-run` / `review-lean` tests:
  - Each CLI call is capped at 180s and writes its output to files rather than pipes.
  - `TRACETOON_REVIEW_TIMEOUT_MS=60000` stops a hung fake reviewer after one minute instead of fifteen.
  - A call that timed out after printing its whole JSON result counts as finished.
- Per-test timeout goes from 30s to 120s. One CLI call takes about 10s on the Windows runner, and a test makes several.
- `test-source.ts` / `test-packaged.ts` exit explicitly after flushing.

**CI**
- `ci.yml`: the test job has `timeout-minutes: 45` instead of GitHub's 6h default.

The branch also merges upstream main (#52, #53, #54, #55); those changes already landed there.

## Validation (Linux, Bun 1.3.14)
- `bun run typecheck`: passed.
- `bun run test`: 48 of 49 files passed. One test in `tests/composition.test.ts` (unchanged on this branch) hit its 90s timeout during the 4-way parallel run while other test suites were loading the host. Run alone (`bun test tests/composition.test.ts`), the file passed 17/17 in 27s.
- `bun run build:check`: not completed here. It needs the git-ignored bundle receipt (`dist/tracetoon.mjs.build.json`), which this checkout doesn't have. The committed bundle and `build.json` were regenerated on the branch.
- `test:bundled` / `test:compiled`: left to CI, which runs the packaged contracts on every platform.
- I couldn't reproduce the Windows behaviour locally; the Windows CI job is the real test.

title: Bound hung test processes and publish to one target repo
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR's purpose is to stop hung test files from holding Windows CI for hours ("Is the windows check hung? 3 hours.") and to fix publishing to the right repository ("Is this issue fixed?", issue 52). Commit f17a0924eef1 says Windows runs hung three times, each in a different test file, with no output until the job was cancelled. Commit fd4c9f7b30d5 attributes those hangs to Bun on Windows not exiting once done. Commit 9da90dccfd02 describes a CLI command that did not exit after its output, and links the earlier whole-file hangs to it. Commit 9af69e8f453c says such CLI processes kept appearing in new test files.

**Test runner.** Previously the runner waited for each file's close event with no limit. It now kills a file after a timeout (15 minutes by default, `TRACETOON_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS`; the whole process tree via taskkill on Windows, the bun process elsewhere) and fails it with the output so far. When a file's summary has appeared and bun has not exited within a grace period (20s by default, `TRACETOON_TEST_EXIT_GRACE_MS`), the runner kills it and judges it by the fail/error counts. A killed child's pipes are destroyed and unref'd, and test-source and test-packaged exit explicitly after flushing. The CI test job gets a 45-minute limit instead of GitHub's 6-hour default. The runner adds a `--timeout` flag to the bun command line; per commit c118cf7891e6, Bun 1.3 ignores the bunfig.toml timeout. Commit db0d81ae0bfa explains that slow process-spawning cases outgrew Bun's 5s default and set 30s; commit e8b441728a5d raised it to 120s. Commit e8b441728a5d expects real hangs to be bounded by the per-file watchdog and the spawn caps.

**CLI exit and test guard.** Previously the entry point relied on a natural exit, so a leftover handle kept the process running. The CLI now flushes output and calls `process.exit` with the command's code; if `TRACETOON_EXIT_FILE` is set it first writes that code there. `tests/spawn-guard.ts` kills a CLI that recorded its code but stays alive (3s later, per commit 9af69e8f453c); commands that exit themselves, or never finish, behave as before. `tests/helpers.ts` mocks node:child_process so spawnSync of the CLI goes through that guard. Commit 2fe71a320c8c says the watchdog caught review-run stalled for 15 minutes on Windows while the tests' spawnSync had no timeout; the review-run and review-lean helpers cap each CLI call, name the command with partial output on timeout, and review-run kills a hung fake reviewer after a minute. Commit e8b441728a5d explains why the helpers write output to files: with pipes, spawnSync on Windows waits for every holder of the pipe, even after `review run --all` printed its result. Per fd4c9f7b30d5, a helper call that timed out with its whole JSON result on stdout counts as finished. Commit db0d81ae0bfa says the merged-list test hard-coded a pass order that depends on which concurrent reviewer finished first, and adjusts it.

**One target repository.** Context, doctor and publish share one target: gh's default repo when it is a remote of this clone, else origin; when origin is a GitHub remote, a stale default matching no remote is ignored. `prTruth` looks up the existing PR in the resolved target. gh calls name it with `--repo`. Render records the target in the approval and prints a 'PR target: ...' line; when the approval recorded a target, publish refuses if it changed since the render. Doctor reports the target and checks push access on origin; comic hosting still pushes to origin while the private-repo check uses the target. When origin is a fork of the target, `gh pr create` gets `--head owner:branch` and the existing-PR lookup keeps PRs whose head lives in that fork; this was found publishing from a fork. Digest and render read `tracetoon check` receipts whenever the run has any; receipt summaries read stderr before stdout, and the environment identity ignores temp-directory and terminal variables. Tests add a fork clone fixture and narrow the comic test's `pr list` match; new test files cover fork PR heads, check summaries and receipts (receipts-and-fork.test.ts), the spawn guard (spawn-guard.test.ts), target choice (target.test.ts) and the runner's kills (test-files.test.ts). The bundle is regenerated.

The gh-flow and target tests replace `gh` with fakes, so they check the logic around those calls, not the real GitHub API. CI results in the logs are for an earlier commit, not this head.

## Validation

- Checks passed on the submitted content: `bun run typecheck`, `bun run test` (Source test files: 49 passed, 0 failed (up to 4 fresh processes)).
- `bun run build:check`: failed, run on the submitted content.

Where to start: `publishImpl` in src/commands/publish.ts, owning the fork `--head` and existing-PR filter; target choice is in `resolveTarget` (src/github/target.ts).

Feedback wanted: is the 20s post-summary grace long enough on loaded Windows runners to avoid killing a bun that is still exiting?

title: Add an evidence graph of how each PR was made, queryable by the agents
body:
## What this adds

Every digest now also builds `evidence-graph.json`, a graph of how the PR was made. It links:

- each prompt to the edits made in its turn
- each edit to the diff hunks its lines survive in
- each test or check run to the PR files edited after it
- each commit to the session that made it

The graph runs in-process on [cypherlite](https://github.com/neo4j-labs/cypherlite) v0.16.1, compiled to WebAssembly. It is vendored in `src/graph/vendor/` and `assets/cypherlite.wasm`, and `build-dependencies.json` pins it by tag, revision and SHA-256. `bun scripts/cypherlite.ts rebuild` reproduces it, and `build:check` refuses mismatched bytes. No native modules, no database file. If the engine can't start, the digest is still written, with a note.

### How it's used

- **`tracetoon query`**: agents can ask named questions (`outline`, `why <path|path:line|H#|diff:N>`, `verified`, `unverified`, `unexplained`, `turn`, `stale`, `dead-ends`, `pushback`, `schema`) or run read-only `--cypher`. Output is TOON (or `--json`), capped per section unless `--all` is given.
- **Digest**: adds per-file facts and the checks that ran after each file's last edit. Budgeting now keeps what explains the PR, not just the most recent entries.
- **Claims, notes, review**: stale test claims name the files edited after the run. Notes get per-change provenance. The reviewer gets `graphLeads` (files no passing check followed, hunks no captured edit explains). The skill tells reviewers these are leads, not findings.
- **Drafters**: the graph is an index, not a substitute for reading. `why` lists every hunk of the target and each commit's message body. The skill still requires reading every behavior hunk and expanding commits that have a message body. `prepare` output now includes a `next` step and a `graphOutline`. `evidence-notes.md` embeds the outline. If no query ran, `render` adds a `graphHint`.

### Fixes that came along

- When one shell command chains several checks (`tsc && bun test`, …), each check is now recorded as its own run. Before, only one run was recorded, so writers said other checks "were not run". A failing exit status is no longer pinned on every check in the chain.
- `digest.json` keeps the full merge-base hash. It used to cut it to 12 characters, so `tracetoon source --revision base` always failed.

## Evidence on effect

To be clear: a prbench dev comparison (Codex Sol/Terra, Claude Opus/Sonnet; 5 cases × 3 replicates) of the first version **found no benefit**. Later commits respond to what that comparison showed:

- Drafters treated the graph as a substitute for reading. In 12 of 12 judgments, Terra drafts dropped a motivation that was in a commit body.
- Sonnet rarely queried the graph: 0 of 15 drafts, then 2 of 5 after the first pointer change.

This PR does not re-run that comparison after the final changes, so it shows no quality improvement. `bun scripts/eval-graph.ts [--synthetic]` measures digest size, fact retention per budget, provenance lookup cost and timings. It does not measure draft quality.

## Checks

On Linux with Bun 1.3.14 (the pinned version):

- `bun run typecheck`: passed
- `bun run test`: 37 source test files passed, 0 failed
- `bun run test:bundled`: 14 packaged contracts verified against the shipped bundle
- `bun run build:check` and `bun scripts/cypherlite.ts check`: passed (4 vendored files match the pin)
- Prettier check on the changed `src/` and `tests/` files: clean
- `bun run test:compiled`: not run locally, left to CI, which runs both packaged suites on every platform

The last commit only rebundles. `build.json` and `dist/tracetoon.mjs` had last been stamped at the first commit, so `build:check` failed and the shipped bundle was missing the later three commits.

title: Add a queryable evidence graph of how each PR was made
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR integrates a lightweight graph database into Tracetoon as a core feature, as asked: "Do a proper feature integration, not just a partial integration, even if it means making architectural changes to tracetoon." The approved plan notes that Tracetoon recomputes the links between sessions, prompts, edits, runs and commits in memory on each run and then discards them; the goal is to keep those links so agents can ask questions of them.

**Design.** When the engine loads, the digest step also builds `evidence-graph.json`: prompts linked to the edits made in their turn, edits to the diff hunks their lines survive in, runs to the PR files edited after them, and commits to the sessions that made them. Per its commit message, the engine runs in-process on cypherlite v0.16.1 compiled to WebAssembly, pinned by hash in build-dependencies.json and rebuilt with scripts/cypherlite.ts, so no native modules are added; the vendored code is excluded from Prettier. A new `tracetoon query` command answers named questions (outline, why, unverified, stale, schema and others) or read-only Cypher, printed as TOON, with `--params` and `--all` (sections otherwise capped at 60 rows). The graph is an index: `why` lists each hunk of the target, marking those no captured edit explains, plus each commit's message body. If the engine cannot start, the digest is still written with a note. `assetsDir` moves to src/util/assets.ts, resolving next to the running script and falling back to the working directory if that lookup throws.

**Consequences.** With relevance from the graph, the digest budget trims least-important content first. Stale test claims name the later-edited files, and the reviewer receives unverified files and unexplained hunks as leads when graph leads exist. `prepare` prints a "Next:" pointer to the graph, and `prepare --json` carries `graphOutline`, capped at 40 rows per section and left out if the graph can't be read. `prepare` output gains a `next` key and "Next:" line pointing at `query outline` and `query why`. evidence-notes.md opens with the same pointer when a graph exists and includes the outline right after it, at digest and again at render. `render` adds `graphHint` when the digest has a graph and no `tracetoon query` ran in the run. The skill and drafter instructions now tell whoever drafts to use the outline and `why`, read each behavior hunk and expand commits with bodies; reviewers treat graph leads as places to look, not findings. Commands that chain several kinds of check now yield a separate record for each kind. Previously digest.json cut the merge base to 12 characters; it keeps the full hash now. The build verifies the vendored engine against its pin, and `doctor` reports whether the engine is available; packaged contracts, docs, tests/graph.test.ts and an offline benchmark (scripts/eval-graph.ts) cover the graph.

Commit db53f4f29cd6's message reports that a prbench dev comparison found no benefit from the graph, that the skill said to navigate by the graph while `why` returned only commit subjects, and that chained checks were mis-recorded so writers claimed checks "were not run"; per that message, Terra drafts dropped a commit-body motivation in 12 of 12 judgments. Commit 14be3ce8765d's message says Sonnet never queried the graph in a prbench comparison (0 of 15 drafts), because it drafts inline from the `prepare` output and evidence-notes.md, and the graph step lived only in the drafter instructions and role-packets.json. Commit ca6ac22d1881's message says pointing at the graph moved Sonnet only to 2 of 5 drafts with any query, hence the embedded outline. The vendored engine, wasm asset and bundle are generated. CI results for the final head are not in the session logs.

**Where to start:** `renderCmd` in src/commands/publish.ts, which adds `graphHint` when the run made no graph query.

**Feedback wanted:** Is the 40-row cap per outline section right for large PRs, or should `prepare --json` carry less of the graph?

## Why

The full reviewer cost about 38% of each draft. Most of that went on reading the workflow doc, the whole brief and the whole patch, then writing `review.json` by hand, which often came out with a placeholder `agentId` or invalid refs. With the lean reviewer, the reviewer reads one packet and reports only its findings. Tracetoon then writes the contract.

## What changes

- **`tracetoon review-packet --lean --run <id> [--json]`** writes `review-packet.md`. It contains:
  - a fingerprint header and the title
  - the rendered body with line numbers, with the generated Validation section left out

  - a map from each hunk to the symbol that owns it

- **`review-findings.json` v1** schema. Validation lists every fix needed, not just the first.
- **`tracetoon review import --run <id> [--findings <path>] [--agent-id <id>]`** writes `review.json` v2, bound to the current review-input fingerprint:
  - records the drafter as inline and the reviewer as delegated
  - refuses placeholder agent ids
  - resolves brief refs and `path:line` to diff refs
  - lists unknown refs as warnings instead of failing
- **`references/reviewer-lean.md`** holds the reviewer's entire instructions.
- The shipped bundle (`dist/tracetoon.mjs`, `build.json`) is rebuilt to include all of the above.

Code: `src/contribution/leanReview.ts`, `src/commands/review.ts`, `src/cli.ts`. Tests: `tests/review-lean.test.ts`.

<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Per the commit message, the full reviewer cost about 38% of each draft, mostly reading the workflow doc, the whole brief and the whole patch, and then writing `review.json` by hand, often with a placeholder agentId or invalid refs. This PR replaces that with a lean reviewer that reads one packet and reports only findings, while Tracetoon writes the review contract itself. It serves a planning request to get the measurement work done faster, where runs are measured in tokens.

**Design.** `tracetoon review-packet --lean` writes `review-packet.md`: a fingerprint header, the title, the line-numbered rendered body with the generated Validation section elided, the open limits, changes, commit messages, tests and requests from the stored evidence, a hunk-to-owning-symbol map, and the diff. The diff is shown whole when the reduced patch is at most 16000 characters; otherwise the packet keeps cited hunks, branching hunks and test assertions. Even when whole, it omits generated, lock and version files (named on an "Omitted files" line) and shows test files only as hunk headers plus added assertions. The reviewer's whole instruction lives in `references/reviewer-lean.md`, which allows at most 3 lookups and adds a confirmation round that re-reads only the changed lines.

The reviewer writes `review-findings.json` (schema v1); validation lists every fix needed rather than stopping at the first error. title: Neighborhood evidence brief layout, and render reports each finding once
body:
## Summary

Adds a new **neighborhood** layout for the evidence brief. Instead of TOON tables, the brief shows the evidence graph as one block per change. This PR also makes `render` stop repeating brief-check findings that the writer can't clear.

### Neighborhood brief layout (`5539230`)
- `TRACETOON_BRIEF_LAYOUT` selects the layout. **`neighborhood` is now the default** (`src/graph/layout.ts`). Setting `TRACETOON_BRIEF_LAYOUT=toon` reproduces the previous brief byte for byte.
- Each change block lists:
  - its requests, with full text shown once
  - its commits, with each sentence's hunks (`→ H#`)
  - each changed file with its hunks, the requests behind them and key changed lines (`- old ⇒ + new`)
- Each hunk keeps up to 24 key changed lines in the graph (`Hunk.code`). Hunks can be cited as `H#` through a new `hunks` section in `briefParts`, so `render` checks those citations.
- Sentence → hunk links are made per hunk and are conservative. A link needs one of: a file the sentence names, each part of a list sentence, a single code hunk that shares words, or `describedHunks` scoring above its tie margin.
- Blocks are packed to a 2,112-token evidence budget (`TRACETOON_BRIEF_BUDGET`):
  - Headers, requests, sentences and file lines are always included.
  - Code lines are added greedily, by value per character.
  - On large PRs, text is clipped and file lines are compacted to fit.
- `tracetoon query brief` prints the same neighborhood text that `prepare` shows.
- The skill references (`quick-path.md`, `contribution-workflow.md`) now explain `→ H#` hunks alongside `implementedBy`.

### Render: report each finding once (`48a90d7`)
- `render` saves the brief-check findings it has already reported (`brief-findings-seen.json` in the run). A finding that an earlier render reported is listed under "repeated" and no longer blocks. Before this change, Codex graph-arm drafts ran `render` up to 44 times. One sentence that attributed a result to the commit message was flagged as a run claim 18 times. The goal-request and change rows were reported as uncovered dozens of times.
- A sentence tagged with the commit message, or that names it, is no longer treated as a run claim.

## Review notes
- **Riskiest part:** the default changes. Once this merges, every brief uses the neighborhood layout unless `TRACETOON_BRIEF_LAYOUT=toon` is set. The code comment still says "default on this branch". Decide whether that's the intended default at merge.
- Suggested starting points: `src/graph/neighborhood.ts` (block building and budget packing) and the sentence → hunk linking in `src/graph/queries.ts` / `src/graph/build.ts`.
- Demoting repeated findings means a finding that is still real stops blocking after it has been shown once. That's intentional, to stop render loops. Feedback is welcome on whether some findings classes should stay blocking.
- The bundle (`plugin/skills/tracetoon/dist/tracetoon.mjs`) and `build.json` are regenerated.

## Validation
Run locally on Linux with Bun 1.3.14:
- `bun run typecheck`: passed.
- `bun run test`: all 39 source test files passed, including the new `tests/neighborhood.test.ts` and the added cases in `tests/render-loops.test.ts`.
- `bun run build:check`: **did not pass.** It stops with "Bundle output receipt is missing", because the local `dist/tracetoon.mjs.build.json` receipt doesn't exist in this checkout. `main` fails the same way here, so this is about the environment, not this branch. The build-identity staleness check before that point passed.
- `bun run test:bundled` / `bun run test:compiled`: not run locally. Left to CI, which runs the packaged contracts on every PR.

title: feat(brief): neighborhood layout for the evidence brief, packed to an evidence budget
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR delivers the evidence graph's changes, requests, commit sentences and hunks to the PR writer as per-change blocks instead of flattened tables, following the approved plan "Neighborhood brief: give the graph arm its budget, delivered as a graph". That plan found the graph brief gave writers too little evidence and showed diff ranges instead of lines, with most commit sentences linked to no code.

**Design.** The writer's evidence text (the "brief" Tracetoon prints) can now be laid out as one neighborhood block per change unit; `TRACETOON_BRIEF_LAYOUT=toon` selects the table layout, and any other value gives the neighborhood layout. The commit message says `toon` reproduces the previous brief byte for byte. Each block shows its requests (full text once, clipped on large PRs), its commits with each sentence's hunks (`→ H#`), and each changed file with its hunks and key changed lines (`- old ⇒ + new`). Hunks keep up to 24 key changed lines in the graph and are citable as `H#` because `briefParts` changed to emit a hunks section, so render checks those refs. Sentence-to-hunk links are hunk level and conservative: a named file, each part of a list sentence, a single code hunk that shares words, or the `describedHunks` scoring with its tie margin; when the two best-fitting hunks are close and in different files, neither is linked. Blocks are packed to an evidence budget (`TRACETOON_BRIEF_BUDGET`, 2,112 tokens by default, estimated as characters ÷ 4): headers, requests, sentences and file lines are kept, and code lines are added greedily by value per character. When the kept lines alone exceed the budget, request and sentence text is clipped to 320, then 200, then 120 characters, and file lines are compacted. The avoid and limits rows stay TOON tables before the blocks, and tests, housekeeping and validation after them. In the neighborhood layout, `tracetoon query brief` prints the same text the writer gets, so `--all` and the row cap no longer apply to it there. tests/neighborhood.test.ts covers key code lines and sentence-to-hunk links.

**Render loop fix.** Render now lists a finding an earlier render of the run already reported under "repeated" without blocking on it (matched by kind and exact text, so a reworded sentence blocks again), and a sentence tagged with or naming a commit message is not treated as a run claim. tests/render-loops.test.ts covers both. Previously a sentence matching the validation pattern was counted as a validation claim even when it attributed the result to a commit message. The commit message cites Codex drafts that ran up to 44 renders because of these repeats.

**Consequences.** The writer references now tell drafters to name the file and the `→ H#` hunks behind a behavior when the brief has them; the `toon` layout has no hunk refs. The bundle and build receipt were rebuilt.

title: Keep shell quoting and <repo> paths in check receipts; make the reviewed brief path the default
body:
## Summary

Two changes:

### 1. Receipt commands keep their shell quoting and show repo paths as `<repo>` (`src/workflow/checks.ts`)

- **Before:** a receipt's command was shown as `command.join(' ')`. So `bash -c 'bun run typecheck && bun test'` came out as `bash -c bun run typecheck && bun test`, which is not the command that ran. The scrubber also removed the repository root from arguments, so a passing retry that used an absolute path looked the same as the failed relative-path attempt before it.
- **After:**
  - The new exported `shellJoin()` quotes any argument that contains spaces or shell characters, using POSIX single quotes (`'` becomes `'\''`, and an empty argument becomes `''`). `receiptEvidence` uses it to build each `cmd`.
  - The new `atRepo()` rewrites paths inside the repository (both the root as given and its `realpath`) to `<repo>/…` before scrubbing. An absolute path stays visibly absolute without exposing the machine path.
  - `commandSha256` is still the hash of the original argv.

### 2. The reviewed brief path is the default when a brief exists (`plugin/skills/tracetoon/SKILL.md`, `src/commands/digest.ts`, `src/commands/publish.ts`)

- When `prepare --json` returns a brief, SKILL.md now defaults to a new **step 2b**. The orchestrating agent writes `change-map.json`, `title.txt` and `body.md` itself from the brief. It runs the required checks once with `tracetoon check` and runs `render --check` until nothing is listed. Then one fresh independent reviewer writes `review.json` v2 (drafter `inline`, reviewer `delegated`). There is one correction round, and the same reviewer confirms it.
- The three-role researcher/drafter/reviewer path is now used only when the user asks for the most thorough PR, or when there is no brief. The quick path (2a) still requires the user to ask for it.
- `graphNext()` (the `next` hint from `prepare`) and the lean-mode messages from `render --check` now point to step 2b instead of "the full path".

## Tests

- `tests/evidence.test.ts`: new test for `shellJoin`. It covers a `bash -c` compound command, a `<repo>` env assignment that is left unquoted, and an embedded single quote.
- `tests/graph.test.ts`: the `prepare` `next` assertions now expect the reviewed brief path, the single fresh independent reviewer, and the quick-path mention.

## Validation

Run locally with Bun 1.3.14:

- `bun run typecheck`: passed
- `bun run test`: passed (37 source test files, 0 failed)

Not run locally; left to CI, which runs these on every PR:
- `bun run test:bundled` and `bun run test:compiled`

## Notes

- `plugin/skills/tracetoon/dist/tracetoon.mjs` is not regenerated in this PR. The committed bundle already predated the recent SKILL/graph commits on `main`, and CI rebuilds it with `bun run bundle`. If reviewers want the bundle committed in the same PR, it should be refreshed before merge (CONTRIBUTING asks for this).
- A comment in `tests/graph.test.ts` (around line 286) still says "the default is the full path", just above the updated comment. It should be removed in a follow-up or before merge.

title: Keep shell quoting in check receipts and make the reviewed brief path the default
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR does what was asked after a step-back review of recent results: "go ahead with the plan" to find the sweet spot for the workflow. It fixes how check receipts record commands and changes which drafting path Tracetoon recommends when an evidence brief exists.

## Check receipts

The commit message traces this to a confirmation round where four of six accuracy flags were Tracetoon's own Validation lines. Previously, receipts joined argv with spaces, so a quoted `bash -c` command read as a different command, and the scrubber stripped the repository root, so a retry with an absolute path was indistinguishable from the earlier relative-path attempt. Now `prepareCheck` stores each argument through a new `atRepo` helper, which writes the repository root, and its resolved real path when that differs, as `<repo>`. `atRepo` replaces the root string wherever it appears, so a sibling path that shares the root as a prefix is rewritten too. `receiptEvidence` joins the stored command with a new `shellJoin`, which single-quotes arguments containing spaces or shell characters other than `<` and `>`, and writes an empty argument as `''`. The new test in tests/evidence.test.ts, "receipt commands keep their shell quoting", covers a `bash -c` command, an argument holding a `<repo>` path and an apostrophe.

Previously, `graphNext` recommended a three-role path: a researcher collected the repository's guidance and a separate drafter wrote the description. With an evidence brief, it now recommends the reviewed path (SKILL step 2b): the coordinating agent finds the required checks itself, drafts change-map.json, title.txt and body.md, runs each check once with `tracetoon check`, fixes what `render --check` lists for up to three rounds, and then one fresh independent reviewer checks the result, with one correction round confirmed by the same reviewer. Without a brief, SKILL.md keeps the researcher, drafter and reviewer roles. In `renderCmd`, the checked-draft issue and the Next line now point at SKILL step 2b.5 instead of "the full path". The commit message bases this on a step-back analysis saying the independent reviewer is the part that wins, while the researcher and drafter subagents add little separable value for their cost. SKILL.md reaches the quick path and the three-role thorough path when the user's own message asks for them. The tests in tests/graph.test.ts now expect the new wording.

title: Lean brief path: Tracetoon writes the Validation section and checks writers' brief citations
body:
## Why

In the benchmark, Claude writers turned brief rows into factual errors, and most of those errors were claims about runs and tests (56–90% of their factual errors). Cheaper writers also dropped the researcher/drafter/reviewer workflow. This branch adds a lean path: Tracetoon writes the run results itself, and writers have to cite the brief for every factual sentence.

## What changes

**Tracetoon writes the Validation section** (`src/graph/briefRender.ts`, `src/commands/publish.ts`)
- `render` fills a Validation section from the brief's validation rows at `<!-- tracetoon:validation -->`, so writers no longer restate run results. There is only one Validation heading, and commands appear without redirections (no more `bun test > <outside-repo>`).
- Each line says only what the logs show. If no edit was logged after a run, the line says it isn't recorded whether the run used the final code. If edits were logged after it, the line names them. If the outcome wasn't logged, the line says the result isn't in the logs. An unreadable result says Tracetoon couldn't read it.
- Long lists end with "and N more", and results don't end with a period.

**Validation rows keep real results** (`src/graph/evidence.ts`, `src/graph/queries.ts`)
- Quoted env assignments before a test command (`X="$(pwd)/a b" bun test`) are skipped, so a second suite isn't missed and its counts don't go to the first suite.
- If several test commands share one output, they still pass when each reports zero failures, but they get no counts because the counts can't be pinned on one command.
- If no run used the final code, the latest run of each kind is kept. Before, map order followed a command's first run instead of its last. `cmd` and `cmd 2>&1` count as the same command.

**Writers cite brief refs, and render checks them** (`src/graph/briefRender.ts`)
- Factual sentences end with brief refs such as `[CH1, S1]`. Render removes the tags and reports these in `render --json` → `briefCheck`:
  - untagged sentences (the message says to delete them or reword them to a row, not just tag them)
  - unknown refs
  - run or test claims outside the Validation section
  - tagged sentences that name code (`fn()`, `a.b`, `src/x.ts`, camelCase) that none of their cited rows mention
- Short commit shas (7+ characters) count as known refs.
- The brief's limits and avoid rows are marked as instructions, never PR text.

**Workflow** (`plugin/skills/tracetoon/SKILL.md`, `src/workflow/readiness.ts`, `src/cli.ts`)

title: Lean brief path: Tracetoon writes the Validation section and checks writers' ref tags
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR aims to make cheap, low-effort writers draft faithfully from Tracetoon's evidence summary, so that a model like Luna "will just write it up" without overthinking. Two failure modes stood in the way: Claude writers turned summary facts into errors, most of them run and test claims, and cheap writers gave up on the researcher/drafter/reviewer workflow.

## Design

When `prepare --json` returns an evidence summary, SKILL.md step 2a and prepare's next text now send the writer down a lean path: draft inline from it and run `render --lean`. The CLI gains the `--lean` option for this. Previously prepare's next text told the writer to draft from the evidence summary; it now also asks for a body order: what changes and why, each change unit, then where to start. When no review was recorded, `render --lean` records it as skipped, and publish accepts a skipped review.

Render writes the Validation section itself from the recorded validation results at the validation marker, so no writer restates run results. Commit ace88af07bb3 reports that Claude judges read the old wording ("ran after the last edit the logs captured") as checking the final code. Now a run with no later edit in the logs says whether it ran on the final code is not recorded, and a run with later edits names them. An unreadable result says Tracetoon could not read it, not that the logs lack it.

Writers tag factual sentences with refs; render strips the tags and reports unknown refs and run or test claims outside the Validation section, plus untagged sentences once a draft uses tags, in `render --json` under `briefCheck`. A tagged sentence that names code none of its cited rows mention is listed as unbacked, and short commit shas of seven or more characters count as known refs. The render message says untagged sentences are to be deleted or reworded, not just tagged. Limits and avoid rows are marked as instructions for the writer rather than PR text, and the branching limit drops its rough line count. Commands in the Validation section drop output redirections, so `cmd` and `cmd 2>&1` count as one command. `renderCmd` in publish.ts now reads the stored graph's brief parts as well.

## Consequences for recorded results

The digest now skips quoted env assignments before test commands, so a second suite is not missed and its counts are not credited to the first. Previously several test commands sharing one output got an unknown outcome; now they pass when each reported zero failures, with counts left off since they can't be pinned on one. With no run on the final code, the latest run of each kind is kept.

## Validation

<sub>From runs on the submitted content.</sub>

- `bun run typecheck`: passed, run on the submitted content.
- `bun run test`: failed (Source test files: 36 passed, 1 failed (up to 4 fresh processes)), run on the submitted content.

**Where to start:** `brief` in src/graph/queries.ts, which supplies the recorded results render writes the Validation section from.

**Feedback wanted:** should a skipped review stay acceptable for publish outside the lean path, or should publish restrict it to runs rendered with `--lean`?

title: feat(review): review run --all, review merge, and the Review recheck setting
body:
## Summary

One command now runs every planned reviewer pass and returns a single merged findings list. The drafter applies all findings in one edit pass, and reviewer rechecks become optional.

- **`tracetoon review run --all`** runs one pass per lens, plus any general passes beyond the lens count. The passes run concurrently, and each slot gets its own packet, reply, findings and reviewed-body files. Each pass is imported the same way a single run is.
  - **Partial failure:** the passes that succeeded are still imported. The command names the failed passes, prints a rerun command, and exits non-zero. The rerun skips passes already imported for the same body.
  - **`--all --recheck`** resumes every pass. With `contested`, it resumes only the passes that have rejected findings. `--note` passes rejections along.
- **`tracetoon review merge`** builds the same merged list from passes that are already imported, for the agent runner.
- **`review-findings-merged.md`:**
  - Duplicate findings are merged when their quotes match after normalization or are near-duplicates. Omissions are matched by evidence instead.
  - The strongest verdict is kept, and claims come before omissions.
  - Each line names its passes. The list is capped at 12.
- **New `Review recheck: once|contested|none` setting:** a SKILL line plus `prepare --review-recheck`. It is stored in `review-plan.json` when it isn't `once`. The publish gate never needs a recheck. The next steps printed by `prepare`, `render` and `review` follow the setting.
- **SKILL step 2b:** one review command (or `merge`), one edit pass, and a recheck only if the setting asks for one. A single `review run` without `--lens` now also works when the plan asks for general passes beyond the lenses.
- **Bundle:** `plugin/skills/tracetoon/dist/tracetoon.mjs` and `build.json` were out of date (they predated the evidence graph). I rebuilt them with `bun run bundle`.

## Tests

New tests are in `tests/merge-findings.test.ts`, `tests/review-run.test.ts` (covering `--all`, partial failure, rerun skipping and recheck modes) and `tests/skill-settings.test.ts`.

<!-- tracetoon:start -->
## Why

This PR came out of the request to "put a plan together for the next code round". Its purpose is that one command handles every planned reviewer slot and returns one merged list, so the drafter applies findings in a single edit pass and reviewer rechecks become optional.

## Design

The `--all` option of `tracetoon review run` starts one reviewer per lens plus the general reviewers beyond the lens count, concurrently, with a separate packet, reply, findings and reviewed-body file for each slot. Previously the per-reviewer file names were keyed by an optional lens; they are now keyed by a slot suffix. Each reviewer's reply is imported as a single review is, and the new `mergeFindings` module combines them into review-findings-merged.md. ## Summary

This ports the SQLite evidence store from `feat/evidence-sqlite` onto the current graph build. It runs alongside cypherlite, and **cypherlite stays the default engine**: `TRACETOON_EVIDENCE_ENGINE=sqlite` switches to SQLite.

title: feat(sql): SQLite evidence store with cypherlite row order, behind TRACETOON_EVIDENCE_ENGINE
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The changes were made while carrying out the approved "Round 14: strong writer, cheap high-effort reviewers" plan for Tracetoon drafting. This PR ports the SQLite evidence store onto the current graph build so the evidence behind a brief can live in SQLite tables as well as in cypherlite, with both engines giving the same answers. The default engine stays cypherlite; setting `TRACETOON_EVIDENCE_ENGINE=sqlite` selects SQLite.

## Design

A shared database interface sits in front of both engines, and `src/graph/store.ts` picks the engine from the environment variable and opens the evidence with it. Each named query and brief derivation the description layout uses now has a SQL form next to its Cypher form, and each engine runs its own form. `tracetoon query` gains a `--sql <query>` option, and `--params` now applies to `--sql` as well as `--cypher`. `doctor` still prints `ready (cypherlite, WebAssembly)` by default, and prints the SQLite label when that engine is selected.

The SQL engine stores lists as JSON text and booleans as 0/1, and decodes them on the way back out. The commit says the SQL forms return rows in the order cypherlite does wherever the TypeScript keeps engine order without sorting, because cypherlite walks relationships newest first. A parity check runs the named questions other than `schema` and `search` against both engines and reports mismatches; it also compares the full description parts in the neighborhood layout. The commit reports that a 728-node real graph differed before the ordering fix and that all 69 real graphs now give identical answers.

Each run's `evidence-graph.json` gains an optional `extras` block (file reads and per-response usage) whenever a run has any, under either engine. With `TRACETOON_EVIDENCE_ENGINE=sqlite`, `saveGraph` also writes `evidence.sqlite` into the run folder for any SQLite client. `query search <words>` is a full-text search over prompts, decisions, plans and commit text that needs the SQLite engine but not the extras flag. With the `TRACETOON_SQLITE_EXTRAS` flag on, descriptions add context, fixes and effort sections, followed by an `extraRules` section that holds the rules. To support it, the Claude adapter records Read, Grep, Glob, LS and NotebookRead calls and the Antigravity adapter records view_file, grep_search and list_dir calls, and read-only shell commands such as `cat`, `sed -n` and `rg` count as reads when the call did not fail and the words are path-shaped; per the commit, parsing is quote-aware and skips flag values, sed scripts and find tests, because naive parsing read those as paths. Context rows show the reads made since the previous surviving edit.

## Consequences

With the variable unset, descriptions are still derived from cypherlite. The SQLite schema adds `failedCommands` session fields, decision answers, hunk conditions, a head-refs table and a node order so plans and decisions are read in graph order. New tests check that both engines answer the named questions the same way (the parity check skips `schema` and `search`), that rows come back in graph-engine order, and that extras show only with the flag.

title: Add `tracetoon update` to upgrade an installed Tracetoon in place
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Tracetoon had no update command: upgrading meant re-running `install.sh` or `install.ps1`. The request was for "an upgrade without a reinstall" from the CLI. This PR adds `tracetoon update`, which looks up releases and installs a newer one over the current install.

## Design

According to the commit message, `applyRelease` verifies SHA-256 checksums and checks that the skill and runtime come from one build. It then swaps in the binary, comic assets and the installed skill copies, and undoes those swaps if a step fails before the old copies are discarded. After that point it re-registers the hooks through the new binary and rewrites the install record; hook trouble is returned as `hooks: false` and does not undo the swap. The new binary has to answer `--version` before it is accepted.

The GitHub lookup reads the newest 30 releases and skips drafts and tags that are not versions. The default pick is the most recently published release in the channel, with the version breaking ties, because GitHub lists rc.10 before rc.2 by tag name. The channel defaults to `latest`, which includes release candidates; `stable` leaves them out of the default pick, and any other channel value is rejected. Without `--to`, an update skips a version that is not newer than the current one; `--to <version>` installs the named release whatever the channel, including an older one, and is the rollback path.

`--check` reports without installing; combined with it, `--exit-code` exits with 10 when a newer release exists. Setting `TRACETOON_DISABLE_UPDATES` to 1 turns the command off. `TRACETOON_UPDATE_URL` points the lookup and downloads at a test server.

## Consequences

`updatable` lets `update` replace a binary that the installer placed. For a plugin or bundle copy, a `TRACETOON_BIN` override, or any other binary, it refuses and explains how to update instead. Both installers now record the method, version, tag and path in `install.json`, and `install.ps1` ignores an error from that write. The Windows installer change only ran on linux/x64, so it has not been seen running on Windows. The README documents `tracetoon update` and `--check`. The tests in `tests/update.test.ts` cover version ordering, release selection and what update may replace. The bundled build was regenerated.

## Validation

<sub>From runs on the submitted content.</sub>

- Checks passed on the submitted content: `bun run typecheck`, `bun run test` (Source test files: 50 passed, 0 failed (up to 4 fresh processes)).
- `bun run build:check`: failed, run on the submitted content.

Where to start: `updateCmd` in `src/commands/update.ts`, which owns the channel choice, the disable switch and the decision whether to install.

Feedback wanted: should the default channel be `latest`, so that release candidates are offered, or `stable`?

title: Recognise the VEX AIM's user serial port and fix short writes in write_user
body:
## Summary

Makes the VEX AIM's user (REPL/console) serial port usable, and fixes short writes on the user port.

### Recognise the AIM's user port
`types_by_location()` only knew how the V5 Brain lays out its interfaces (0 = system, 2 = user). The AIM (PID `0x0700`) is a composite device with a UVC camera on interfaces 2 and 3, so its serial ports are on interfaces **0 and 4**. Interface 4 landed in the "Unknown location" branch and was dropped. As a result `find_devices()` returned the AIM with `user_port() == None`, and `read_user()`/`write_user()` quietly fell back to the system port.

- Interface 4 on the AIM is now treated as the user port.
- `types_by_location()` now returns `None` when it recognises no ports, so the name-based fallbacks in `find_ports()` can run. Before, it returned `Some(empty)` and the fallbacks were skipped.

### Write the whole buffer in `write_user`
On the user port, `SerialConnection::write_user()` made a single `AsyncWrite::write()` call. That call may accept only part of the buffer, but the partial count went back to the caller and the port was never flushed. It now calls `write_all()` and then `flush()`, and returns the full length. This matches what the system-port `send()` path already does.

## Tests
New unit tests for `types_by_location()` in `serial.rs`:
- AIM interfaces 0 and 4 map to System and User
- Brain interfaces 0 and 2 still map to System and User
- unrecognised ports return `None`, so the fallbacks run

On macOS, `serialport` reports the CDC data interface (communication + 1), so the test helper adjusts the interface numbers to match what each OS reports.

**Not run:** I couldn't run `cargo test` because Cargo isn't installed in the environment where this PR was prepared. The changes also haven't been tried on real AIM hardware.

title: fix: recognise the VEX AIM user serial port and write the whole user-port buffer
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The purpose of this PR, as requested, is to "submit the PR to the vex-v5-serial project for the bug with the serial ports on the vex aim devices".

Previously `types_by_location()` mapped locations by the V5 Brain layout alone, where interface 0 is the system port and interface 2 is the user port. Per the commit message and code comment, the AIM enumerates as a composite device with a UVC camera on interfaces 2 and 3, so its two serial ports are interfaces 0 and 4. According to the commit message, interface 4 fell into the "Unknown location" branch and was dropped, so the AIM was found with no user port and user reads and writes silently went to the system-port fallback.

## Design

- When the device PID is the AIM's (0x0700) and the location is interface 4, `types_by_location()` treats that port as the user port and logs a debug line; every other location, on the AIM or any device, still goes through the existing Brain mapping.
- When it recognises no port by location, for any device, `types_by_location()` now returns `None` instead of an empty result, so that, per the commit message, the name-based fallbacks in `find_ports()` can run.
- Previously `write_user()` used a single `write()` on the user port, which may accept only part of the buffer, and returned that partial count without flushing. It now uses `write_all()` plus `flush()` and returns the full length, which the commit message says matches the system-port `send()` path.

Inline unit tests in `serial.rs` cover the AIM layout (interfaces 0 and 4), the unchanged Brain layout (0 and 2), and unrecognised ports yielding `None`. The test helper feeds interface numbers the way each OS reports them, because `serialport` reports the CDC data interface (communication + 1) on macOS and `types_by_location()` subtracts 1 there.

## Limits

The macOS interface offset path is unverified on macOS. CI results for the final head are not in the session logs.

title: vexaim: snap command, exec truncation hint, Linux release binary, API reference, CI
body:
## Summary

Adds the following to the `vexaim` CLI and its packaging:

- **`vexaim snap [-o FILE]`** takes one 640x480 MJPEG frame from the AIM's USB (UVC) camera using `nokhwa` (V4L2, Media Foundation or AVFoundation, depending on the OS). It looks for cameras whose name contains "AIM" and tries each one, because only one of the robot's two video nodes streams. It throws away the first frames while auto-exposure settles, then strips the driver's zero padding before writing the JPEG. With `--json` it prints `{ok, path, width, height, bytes}`.
- **Truncation hint:** if an `exec` times out after printing about 1.5 KB or more, the output now includes `possible_output_truncation` and a human-readable hint. The robot's USB buffer drops output after about 2 KB in a single burst.
- **Release binary:** `skill/vex-aim/bin/linux-x86_64/vexaim`, with its `SHA256SUMS`.
- **API reference:** `skill/vex-aim/references/api.md`, plus the raw dump at `build/api-dump.json`.
- **CI:** `.github/workflows/build.yml` builds and tests on a matrix: linux-x86_64, windows-x86_64, macos-arm64 and macos-x86_64. It uploads the binaries and checksums as artifacts. The workflow is marked UNTESTED on CI.
- **`scripts/setup-upstream.sh`** makes the upstream checkout reproducible: it checks out `vexide/vex-v5-serial` at the pinned commit `b3a712a` and applies `patches/0001-aim-user-port-and-write-all.patch`.
- **Sample frames:** `build/cam/vexaim-snap{1,2}.jpg`.

## Testing

- `trim_jpeg` has unit tests in `crates/vexaim-cli/src/snap.rs`.
- Linux x86_64 is the only platform tested on real hardware (see `docs/hardware-test-report.md`). Windows and macOS camera access has not been tested.
- **Not run when this PR was opened:** `cargo build` and `cargo test`. Cargo isn't installed in the environment used to open the PR, and `upstream/` isn't checked out there. The CI workflow should cover both.
- I checked that the committed binary matches the checksum in `SHA256SUMS` (`537484cc…`).

title: vexaim: add snap command, truncation hint, multi-platform CI build and API reference
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To let the `vexaim` CLI see through the robot's camera and explain lost output on timed-out runs, this PR adds a `snap` subcommand, a truncation hint, a cross-platform CI build, a pinned upstream setup script and an API reference for the AIM REPL.

**Camera snapshot.** `vexaim snap [-o FILE]` treats the robot's camera as an ordinary USB webcam through the new `nokhwa` dependency. It lists cameras, keeps those whose lowercased name contains "aim", and errors out with the names it did find when none match. For each match it opens a 640x480 MJPEG stream, skipping nodes that fail to open because the AIM exposes two video nodes and only one streams, reads eight frames so auto-exposure settles, trims trailing zero padding from the driver buffer and writes the JPEG. Without `-o` the file is named `vexaim-snap-<unix-time>.jpg` in the current directory; a non-MJPEG frame is an error. JSON mode reports path, width, height and byte count. On macOS and Windows the user may need to allow camera access for the app, and the no-camera error says so.

**Truncation hint.** Previously a timed-out `exec` printed the "[timed out after Ns]" line with no hint and no truncation field. Now, when the run timed out and stdout reached 1500 bytes, human output adds a hint about the robot's ~2 KB USB buffer overflow and the JSON `possible_output_truncation` field, now present on every exec result, is true; otherwise it is false.

**Build and setup.** A new `build` workflow, triggered on push and manual dispatch, installs `libudev-dev` and `pkg-config` on Linux, then builds and tests the CLI on Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64, macOS arm64 and macOS x86_64 and uploads each binary with a SHA256SUMS file. `scripts/setup-upstream.sh` clones `vex-v5-serial`, checks out a pinned commit and applies the AIM user-port patch from `patches/`. `skill/vex-aim/references/api.md` lists the names the robot's firmware exposes; signatures come from VEX's public AIM docs. A Linux x86_64 release binary, sample snapshots and a regenerated `build/api-dump.json` are committed alongside.

**Limits.** No run of the new workflow appears in this work, Linux job included, and the Windows, macOS and arm64 jobs are not shown running anywhere; the workflow's header comment says Linux x86_64 is the only platform verified on real hardware. No session ran the setup script itself. The two `trim_jpeg` unit tests exercise the padding trim, not camera capture.


Where to start: `snap` in `crates/vexaim-cli/src/snap.rs` (camera selection, frame capture, JPEG trim).

Feedback wanted: is matching cameras by an "aim" substring in the device name reliable enough across Windows and macOS, or should we match by USB vendor/product ID?

title: Find AIM REPL on USB iface 4; 10/10 round trips; experimental upload tools
body:
## Summary

Locates the VEX AIM MicroPython REPL on **USB interface 4** and shows it works reliably, plus a few experimental tools for loading and uploading programs.

### REPL findings
- The REPL takes CRLF-terminated lines and echoes input back (`build/run2.log`). Sending bare tokens with no line ending gets no response (`build/run1.log`).
- `tests/pingpong.py` passed **10/10** `PING`→`PONG` round trips on `/dev/ttyACM1`, at about 50.2 ms each (min 50.2, max 50.3). Results are in `build/pingpong-run1.json`.
  - The probe builds the reply by concatenation (`"AIM_AGENT_V1 "+"PONG"`), so the echoed input can't be mistaken for real output.

### New tools
- `tests/capture.py`, `tests/repl.py`, `tests/pingpong.py`: pyserial scripts for capturing raw serial traffic, sending REPL lines one at a time, and measuring round-trip latency.
- `crates/vexaim-probe`:
  - `dirlist`: **read-only**. Lists files for each `FileVendor`, sending only FILE_DIR / FILE_DIR_ENTRY.
  - `aimload`: sends FILE_LOAD run/stop on vendor User. Stop uses the name `"null"`, the same as VAIMRC-Console.
  - `aimupload`: **EXPERIMENTAL**. Writes `slot_N.ini` + `slot_N.bin` to vendor User and does not run the program. The file format is a guess based on cargo-v5 PR#22 (`ExtensionType::Vm`) and VAIMRC-Console.
  - Turns on the `file-commands` feature of `vex-v5-serial`.
- `refs/VAIMRC-Console` and `refs/aim-ai` are added as reference gitlinks.

## Notes for reviewers
- `refs/*` are gitlinks, but the repo has no `.gitmodules`, so `git submodule update` won't fetch them. Either add `.gitmodules` entries or drop them.
- `build/` holds committed run artifacts (`main.mpy`, logs, the ping-pong JSON) that are kept on purpose as evidence. Consider whether they belong in the repo long-term.
- `aimupload`/`aimload` write to and control the robot. Run them only on a robot you have exclusive use of.

## Test plan
- [x] Python scripts parse (`ast.parse`)
- [ ] `cargo build` for `vexaim-probe`: **not run**. This environment has no `cargo` toolchain and no `upstream/` checkout, which the `vex-v5-serial` path dependency needs.
- [ ] Hardware runs (10/10 ping-pong, REPL capture) were recorded in the committed `build/` artifacts. They were not re-run here because no robot was attached.

title: Add AIM REPL ping-pong scripts and experimental USB file tools
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR records how to reach the VEX AIM's MicroPython REPL over USB and adds small tools for exercising it and the robot's file system, as described in the commit message "Find AIM REPL on USB iface 4; 10/10 round trips; experimental upload tools". The REPL lives on USB interface 4 per that commit message; the diff itself only shows the serial port path used in the recorded run.

**REPL scripts.** `tests/pingpong.py` sends Ctrl-C to get a clean prompt, then runs N round trips (default 10) that each write `print("AIM_AGENT_V1 "+"PONG")` and wait up to 2 s for the evaluated output followed by a `>>>` prompt. The string is concatenated so the echoed input can never match the expected reply. The script prints a JSON result, adding min/max/mean latency when at least one trip succeeded. `tests/repl.py` sends arbitrary lines with CRLF and prints what comes back, using a `drain` helper that reads for a fixed time window; `tests/capture.py` logs everything received and optionally sends lines after 4 s, with the line ending set by the `EOL` environment variable.

**Recorded output.** `build/pingpong-run1.json` records a 10-trip run on `/dev/ttyACM1` with 10 of 10 trips succeeding and a mean latency of 50.2 ms. `build/run1.log` and `build/run2.log` hold raw captures; `run2.log` shows the REPL answering bare `PING` with a `NameError`.

**USB file tools (Rust, `vexaim-probe`).** `dirlist` is read-only: it sends only directory count and entry requests for six file vendors and lists up to 64 entries each. `aimload` sends a FILE_LOAD on vendor User to run a slot file (default `slot_1.bin`) or, for `stop`, sends the name `null`, matching VAIMRC-Console per its header comment. `aimupload` is marked EXPERIMENTAL in its header, for instructor-approved use on an exclusive robot: for a slot from 1 to 8 it writes `slot_N.ini` (Binary type) and `slot_N.bin` (`vm` type unless `bin` is given) to vendor User on the QSPI target, and does not run the program. All three tools connect to the first device `serial::find_devices()` returns, so with several robots attached the write goes to whichever is listed first. Its header comment calls the format a hypothesis built from cargo-v5 and VAIMRC-Console. To support these, the `vex-v5-serial` dependency now enables the `file-commands` feature, and the lockfile was updated. `refs/VAIMRC-Console` and `refs/aim-ai` are added as reference subprojects.


Where to start: `main` in `crates/vexaim-probe/src/bin/aimupload.rs`, which builds the `.ini` and uploads both slot files.

Feedback wanted: should `aimupload` stay in the crate while its file format is still a hypothesis, or move behind an opt-in feature until a robot confirms it?

title: Replug runs: recovery gate met, disconnect/no-robot error messages, kicker verified
body:
## Summary

Adds the unplug/replug hardware runs and the small CLI fixes they turned up.

- **Replug results:** run 1 was done without the udev rule; runs 2–4 were done with `99-vex-aim.rules` installed. JSONL logs are in `docs/replug-run*.jsonl`, and the write-up is in `docs/hardware-test-report.md`.
  - The robot recovered in 20/20 cycles, so the Gate 2 replug criterion is **met**. With the rule installed, recovery took about 0.7–1.7 s after a stable replug.
  - Without the rule, ModemManager probing made recovery slower (up to 14 s) and caused some follow-up round trips to fail.
  - In runs 2–4, every cycle that wasn't fully clean came from how the test was paced: either the cable was pulled for the next cycle while the last follow-up was still running, or the cable bounced. I checked each one against the kernel log.
- **`vexaim` CLI (`crates/vexaim-cli/src/repl.rs`):**
  - With no robot plugged in, the CLI used to show "Could not infer serial port types". It now says no VEX device was found.
  - If the robot disconnects mid-command (broken pipe, no such device or EIO), the CLI now says the robot disconnected and that a movement command may or may not have run. A unit test covers this.
  - The Linux x86_64 binary and its `SHA256SUMS` are rebuilt to match.
- **Kicker:** `kicker.kick(SOFT)` ran and a person confirmed the kicker moved. This is recorded in the report and in `references/api.md`.
- **Skill docs (`SKILL.md`):** documents how the robot behaves after a replug, adds the kicker to the tested list, updates the list of untested items (turns, other kicker actions, Windows/macOS, …), and explains camera orientation: the image follows how the robot is physically sitting, and `snap` never rotates it.
- **Test tools:**
  - `tests/replug.py` is a replug test with sound cues for the person at the robot. It doesn't use any actuators.
  - `tests/stress.py` runs N back-to-back `exec` calls. On 100 calls it got 100/100, averaging 0.72 s per call.

## Testing

- The hardware results are in the report and logs above. They come from the commits on this branch and could not be re-run here.
- In this environment:
  - `py_compile` passes on `tests/replug.py` and `tests/stress.py`.
  - `sha256sum -c` matches the shipped `vexaim` binary.
  - `cargo` is **not available**, so the Rust unit tests (including the new `disconnect_errors_are_recognised`) were **not run** here.

title: Record replug and kicker hardware runs; report USB disconnects and no-robot clearly
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR records the hardware tests requested at the robot: retry the kicker, run unplug/replug cycles, and account for the test robot sitting upside down when judging camera frames. It also fixes the two error messages those runs exposed.

**Disconnects and missing robots.** When a serial I/O error text contains "broken pipe", "no such device" or "input/output error", `vexaim` now says the robot disconnected during the command, that output may be incomplete and that a move may or may not have run, so the robot should be checked before re-running anything; other I/O errors keep the generic "serial I/O error" text. Previously `devices()` mapped any device-discovery error into an I/O error, so an unplugged robot surfaced as the library's "Could not infer serial port types". That one library error now yields an empty device list, so the caller reports no robot found; other discovery errors still return an I/O error. A unit test, `disconnect_errors_are_recognised`, checks that broken-pipe and no-such-device errors match and a timeout does not.

**Replug results.** `tests/replug.py` drives the cycles, logs to JSONL and beeps when it is safe to unplug; the four logs are committed. Run 1, without the udev rule, recovered 5/5 but was only 3/5 fully clean, and the report attributes the slow cycles to ModemManager probing via the journal. Runs 2-4 with the udev rule `99-vex-aim.rules` installed (ModemManager ignore plus `uaccess`) recovered 15/15, mostly in 0.7-1.7 s; one cycle logged 16.9 s, which the report attributes to a cable bounce, and it explains the three non-clean cycles as an unplug cutting off the last follow-up round trip. The report marks the Gate 2 replug criterion as met (20/20 over four runs, 15/15 with the rule). `tests/stress.py` adds a steady-state loop of `vexaim exec` round trips.

**Skill docs.** The skill now says camera orientation follows how the robot physically sits and that `vexaim snap` does not rotate the frame. It lists `kick(SOFT)` as run with a human confirming movement, describes replug behaviour (its "20/20 ... with the udev rule installed" wording also counts the no-rule run 1), and adds Windows and macOS to the not-yet-tested list alongside harder kicks, `place`/`push` and turns.

The replug numbers are Linux-only; Windows and macOS replug behaviour remains unknown.

title: Add the vex-aim agent skill and report MicroPython and Python versions in doctor
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR makes `skill/vex-aim/` the thing you hand to a student: copy the folder into Goose's or Claude Code's skills directory, and the agent gets what it needs to drive a USB-connected VEX AIM robot with the bundled `vexaim` CLI. The skill has to work for an agent that knows nothing else about the robot, so it puts the hardware gotchas up front instead of leaving them to be found by trial and error.

## Design

`SKILL.md` tells the agent to run `vexaim doctor` first, then use `vexaim exec` to run MicroPython. It notes that `exec` already supplies the `vex_globals` imports, so `--no-preamble` is for callers who know why they need it. It also lists the issues seen on the real robot: the ~2 KB output burst limit, a heading-0 position frame, a camera that may come back upside-down, and the MicroPython-versus-Python version question. `references/troubleshooting.md` starts from `vexaim doctor` and maps its failures to causes and fixes, and `references/examples.md` adds starter programs, such as one that reads `robot.inertial.get_heading()`. The Linux udev files now live under `skill/vex-aim/linux/`, so they travel with the skill. On Linux, `sh linux/install-udev.sh` has to be run once with sudo so ModemManager leaves the robot's ports alone.

`doctor` changed to support that version answer. Previously it reported only `sys.version` under a `micropython` key. Now it reports `micropython_core` (the first three parts of `sys.implementation.version`, joined with dots) and `python_compat` (`sys.version` up to the first `;`), so an agent asked "what Python version" can give both numbers. According to the commit message, a later cold test went cleanly: a fresh agent with only the skill completed the student task without failures.

## Consequences

This PR deletes the `refs/` submodule entries and adds `refs/` and `.claude/` to `.gitignore`. A new top-level README covers the layout, the build (`setup-upstream.sh` and then a `cargo build --release`), and current status. Per the README, only the linux-x86_64 binary is built and tested so far, and Windows/macOS builds have not been done. The hardware test report gets a second table for REPL tooling, actuators, the camera and the skill. It records a FAIL for unpaced output over ~2 KB (a robot firmware limit) and NOT RUN for turns, the kicker and unplug/replug.

## Validation

- `cargo build --release --manifest-path crates/vexaim-cli/Cargo.toml`: could not run in this environment (the command was not found); it got no result on the code.
